transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, I guess what finally got me here is this historical society fundraiser thing. I sort of took it on like I was going to run the whole thing myself—quilts and all, because I do know a bit about quilt patterns, my aunt used to make these beautiful ones with tiny little blue squares—but anyway, I started designing quilts, calling volunteers, making schedules, telling people we’d have things done by certain dates… and then I realized I’d promised deadlines I really couldn’t possibly meet. It got away from me.
During that time, did you feel unusually energized or “up” compared with your normal self?

Yes, I did. I mean, I didn’t think of it that way at first—I thought I was just being productive, you know? But I had so much energy I couldn’t even sit through a TV show with my husband. I’d keep jumping up to measure fabric or write down some idea, or I’d suddenly need to rearrange all the supplies. He’d say, “Are you going to watch this or not?” and I’d be halfway to the dining room already.
While this was going on, did you need less sleep than usual?

Yes… yes, definitely. For a while there I was only sleeping a few hours, and then I’d wake up like it was morning even if it really wasn’t, ready to sew or start making phone calls—though of course you can’t call people too early, my mother always said nothing before 9 unless somebody’s dead.

But now it’s sort of flipped around. I’ll lie awake worrying about everything I didn’t finish, or I’ll sleep late and still feel completely worn out.
During that high-energy time, did you feel more confident or capable than usual?

Oh, yes… I really did. I honestly thought my heritage quilt ideas were going to put our little town on the map. Like I’d finally found the one thing that only I could pull off, you know? Which sounds a little much now, saying it out loud, but at the time it felt completely obvious.
During that high-energy time, did you have any experiences like hearing or seeing things that other people didn’t, or believing something that others said wasn’t true?

I don’t… I don’t think so. Not like seeing people in the room or hearing voices, if that’s what you mean.

I mean, I had strong feelings about what I was doing, and I got a little carried away with the quilt idea—my sister said I was talking like I’d already been interviewed by the newspaper, which… well, our local paper will print just about anything if there’s a good photo. They once did a whole piece on the church rummage sale tables. But no, I don’t remember anything like seeing or hearing things other people couldn’t.
During that high-energy period, did your behavior cause serious problems in your life, like at home, work, or with other people?

Yes… it did, though I didn’t want to admit that at first. My husband had to start taking over the regular household things because I just wasn’t keeping up with them, or I’d start one thing and then go off on another idea.

And the historical society… oh, that was embarrassing. I’d promised people things, meetings, quilt pieces, follow-up calls—there’s always someone waiting on something over there, and they keep little notebooks, you know, very organized women. My husband ended up dealing with them because I just couldn’t face everyone once I realized I’d dropped so many commitments.
About how long did that high-energy period last before it changed?

It lasted… longer than I realized at the time. I think about five months, give or take, that whole overdriven stretch with the historical society and the quilt project.

It’s funny, because when you’re in it, it doesn’t feel like a “period,” it just feels like life has finally gotten interesting. And then suddenly everyone else is looking at you like you’ve knocked over the punch bowl at a church supper. But yes… about five months before it really fell apart.
Have you ever had a period lasting at least two weeks when you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day?

Yes… definitely more than two weeks. Since the orders fell behind and all those volunteer conflicts blew up, I’ve just been in this low, guilty place.

It’s been about nine months now, I think. I keep thinking if I could just sort one thing out—one apology, one box of paperwork, one awkward phone call—then maybe it would lift, but it hasn’t really. It’s just sort of been there most days.
During this low period, have you lost interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?

Yes… I have. I used to love going out and checking on my garden, seeing what was coming up, fussing over the little things. And my quilt pieces too—I’d sit with fabric and ideas and lose track of time.

Lately I just look at the fabric, or those seed catalogs when they come in, and… nothing much. I mean, I still know I used to enjoy it. I can remember enjoying it. But it’s like looking at someone else’s hobby sitting there on the table.
During this low period, have you had thoughts that life isn’t worth living or that you’d be better off dead?

I… yes, I have thoughts like that. Not like I’ve made a plan to hurt myself or anything, I haven’t. It’s more… I catch myself thinking maybe it would be easier if I just didn’t wake up.

And then I feel awful even saying that, because my sister would probably say, “Don’t talk nonsense,” and she already has enough on her plate with her roof and those insurance people—good grief, they make everything ten times harder. But the thought is there sometimes, like… nobody would have to deal with my mess anymore.
